INTRODUCTION
Increasing the amount of electricity generated in the United States to power electric vehicles, data centers,
and other end uses, while simultaneously reducing greenhouse gas emissions will require deploying a massive
number of renewable energy faciliDes at an unprecedented scale and pace. Although many renewable energy
faciliDes are sited without a problem, local opposiDon ogen arises. The Sabin Center’s annual report,
Opposi@on to Renewable Energy Facili@es in the United States, documents legal obstacles and challenges that
arise during the siDng process. In parDcular, the report focuses on: (a) state laws and local ordinances
(“restricDons”) that impede the siDng and deployment of uDlity-scale solar, wind, baWery storage projects, and
related transmission projects; as well as (b) instances of organized opposiDon to individual projects (i.e.,
“contested projects”). This ediDon builds on four previous ediDons of our report, adding developments that
occurred between January 1, 2024 and December 31, 2024.

The June 2025 ediDon of this report ﬁnds that severe restricDons, including outright bans and de facto bans on
siDng renewable energy faciliDes, as well as controversies over individual projects, are becoming more
prevalent—parDcularly at the local level. By the end of 2024, at least 459 coun>es and municipali>es across
44 states had adopted severe local restric>ons on siDng renewables. This tally represents an increase of 16%
in the prevalence of local restricDons in just one year; the June 2024 ediDon of this report idenDﬁed 395
counDes and municipaliDes in 41 states that had adopted severe local restricDons by the end of 2023. This
2025 ediDon further idenDﬁes 498 contested projects in 49 states, an increase of 32% over last year’s ediDon,
which idenDﬁed 378 contested projects in 47 states. AddiDonally, this report documents 20 signiﬁcant state-
level restric>ons in 16 states, a tally that has remained roughly constant. Importantly, while the report
includes all of the qualifying restricDons and controversies the authors have idenDﬁed, it does not purport to
be exhausDve.

To provide the public with easier access to the data behind this report, the Sabin Center has launched a new
website, Opposi>on Report (opposiDonreport.org), which oﬀers interacDve maps and data ﬁles for download.1
The data ﬁles include informaDon about project type, status, capacity, and acreage, as well as dates relevant to
restricDons or projects (e.g., date adopted or date cancelled).

Background
Over the coming decades, the United States will need to drasDcally scale up electricity generaDon, while
simultaneously reducing greenhouse gas emissions. A recent study by S&P Global Commodity Insights found
that electricity demand is likely to grow by 35-50% from 2024 to 2050, due to a combinaDon of factors,
including the increasing electriﬁcaDon of the country’s transportaDon and heaDng systems, as well as the

addiDon of new industrial loads, such as data centers, cryptocurrency mining faciliDes, and chip factories.2
MeeDng increased demand while achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 will require the rapid buildout of vast
numbers of new renewable energy faciliDes. Some studies have esDmated that the United States may need to
install as much as 100 GW of new zero-emissions sources each year unDl 2050 to achieve net-zero emissions
under these circumstances,3 while other studies have esDmated that the United States will need to install
approximately 80 GW per year.4 For context, in 2024, the United States added 56 GW of new generaDon and
storage capacity to the grid, including 49 GW from solar, baWery, storage, and wind.5

While 2024 was a year of record-breaking success for the deployment of uDlity-scale renewables in the United
States, three recent studies suggest that installaDons could have been signiﬁcantly higher absent restricDve
zoning and local opposiDon. First, a survey and report published by researchers from Lawrence Berkeley
NaDonal Laboratory in January 2024 found that at least 30% of wind and solar projects were being canceled
ager the submission of a siDng applicaDon.6 When researchers asked developers why these projects were
canceled, the developers cited “local ordinances or zoning” and “community opposiDon” as two of the three
leading causes.7 Second, a study published by USA Today in February 2024 found that 15% of counDes are
eﬀecDvely oﬀ-limits to wind or solar or both.8 Third, a study by researchers from the NaDonal Renewable
Energy Laboratory found that setback requirements alone “can reduce wind and solar resources by up to 87%
and 38%, respecDvely, depending on the size of the setbacks applied.”9 CollecDvely these studies demonstrate
the cumulaDve impact of the types of restricDons and instances of opposiDon described by this report.

Looking ahead, while the U.S. Energy InformaDon AdministraDon predicted as recently as February 2025 that
93% of new capacity installed in 2025 would be solar, wind, and baWery storage, changes in federal siDng, tax,
and other policy may have a dampening eﬀect on renewable energy deployment over the next year and

Our Criteria for Determining if a State Law or Local Ordinance Is “Restric<ve”
This report only includes state laws and local ordinances that are so severe that they either (a) scuWled a
speciﬁc project or (b) could have the eﬀect of barring or signiﬁcantly curtailing renewable energy development
within the relevant jurisdicDon, whether permanently or temporarily. More speciﬁcally, this report considers
any of the following to be “restricDve”:

        1.       any ban on renewable energy facilities, whether permanent or temporary, and whether
                 complete or partial (e.g., no solar on agricultural land);

        2.       any cap on renewable energy facilities (e.g., no more than 1,000 acres or 1% of county land);

        3.       any restriction on the use of energy (e.g., ordinances that allow production for on-site use
                 only);

        4.       any restriction designed to block a particular project;

        5.       any viewshed limitation that is not feasible (e.g., facility must not be visible from roads);

        6.       any requirement that wind turbines be set back (a) more than 1,000 feet (305 meters) or more
                 than 2x maximum blade tip height from property lines or roads; or (b) more than 1,500 feet
                 (457 meters) or more than 3x maximum blade tip height from off-site structures;

Because this report focuses on obstacles to siDng renewable energy faciliDes, policies related to other issues
that aﬀect renewable energy—such as net metering, renewable energy standards, and tax credits—are not
discussed.

Our Criteria for Determining Whether a Project Is a “Contested Project”
For purposes of this report, “contested projects” are deﬁned as those that have faced signiﬁcant opposiDon by
individual residents, community-based groups, or other organizaDons. Signiﬁcant opposiDon is deﬁned to
include the organizaDon of one or more opposiDon groups, the circulaDon of a peDDon, intervenDon in
administraDve proceedings, and/or the ﬁling of lawsuits to block the contested project at issue. In many cases
documented in this database, opponents have succeeded in delaying a contested project’s approval, scaling
down its size, or achieving its cancellaDon.

Key Findings
Local and state restricDons, as well as controversies over individual projects, are numerous and widespread. As
of December 2024, there were at least 459 counDes and municipaliDes with severe local restricDons in 44
states, as well as 498 contested projects in 49 states. The 459 local governments with restricDons included 248
with solar restricDons, 298 with wind restricDons, 18 with baWery storage restricDons, and 5 with transmission-
related restricDons.18 The 498 contested projects include 262 projects with a solar component, 212 with a
wind component, 26 with a storage component and 16 with a transmission component.19 By the end of 2024,
severe restricDons or contested projects were found in every state except Alaska, as shown in Figure 1 below,
with two states, Arkansas and Montana, seeing their ﬁrst local restricDons.

At the state level, signiﬁcant developments in 2024 included: (1) the passage of a law in Florida banning
oﬀshore wind in state waters and banning onshore wind turbines within 1 mile of the coast;21 (2) the passage
of laws in MassachuseWs and Minnesota to streamline renewable energy siDng;22 and (3) liDgaDon challenging
the implementaDon of a 2023 law in Michigan that gives the Michigan Public Service Commission the authority
to preempt local restricDons under certain circumstances.23

In addiDon, this report has conDnued to track the implementaDon of Senate Bill 52 of 2021 (S.B. 52) in Ohio, a
law that allows Ohio’s counDes to adopt binding resoluDons to create restricted areas where large wind energy
projects or solar energy projects (or both) are prohibited. This ediDon idenDﬁed 26 counDes with such
restricDons, which collecDvely account for approximately 30% of Ohio’s 88 counDes. However, the rate at
which counDes are creaDng their ﬁrst restricted areas appears to be slowing down. The report ﬁnds that only 3
counDes created their ﬁrst restricted areas in 2024, compared to 10 counDes in 2023 and 12 counDes in 2022.
See Figure 3 below for a list of Ohio counDes that have adopted restricted areas.

Finally, in 2024, a diverse array of plainDﬀs conDnued to pursue federal lawsuits and appeals challenging the
approval of oﬀshore wind projects. Projects facing these acDons in 2024 included South Fork Wind, RevoluDon
Wind, Vineyard Wind, MarWin, and Coastal Virginia Oﬀshore Wind. Meanwhile, plainDﬀs dropped a lawsuit
challenging the Ocean Wind 1 project as moot, following the project’s cancellaDon in 2023 for economic
reasons. To date, the plainDﬀs in these lawsuits have been unsuccessful in persuading courts to overturn
approvals, and opponents of oﬀshore wind may be resDng their hopes on acDons by the federal execuDve
branch or Congress.

does not purport to be exhausDve. For addiDonal resources about local restricDons and contested projects,
please see the Appendix at the end of this report, which provides informaDon about (1) other databases of
restricDons and instances of community opposiDon and (2) other studies assessing the impacts of local
restricDons, lawsuits, and other forms of community opposiDon on renewable energy development.

     ● Cherokee County: In 2014, the Alabama state legislature enacted S.B. 402, which established certain
       restrictions on wind power in Cherokee County, including: (1) a noise limit of 40 decibels (dBA) at the

     ● DeKalb County: In DeKalb County, wind turbines must be set back 2,500 feet from property lines and
       noise must not exceed 40 decibels. In addition, any wind energy system or turbine “that does not
       operate continuously for 365 consecutive days may be deemed abandoned and shall be removed by
       the operator of the system.”26

     ● Etowah County: In 2014, the Alabama state legislature enacted S.B. 403, which established certain
       restrictions on wind power in Etowah County, including: (1) a noise limit of 40 decibels (dBA) at the
       nearest property line; and (2) a setback of at least 2,500 feet from the nearest property line.27

3.3 Contested Projects
     •   Black Mesa Pumped Storage Project (Apache and Navajo Counties): The developer Nature and People
         First has sought to develop a 6,000-MW, utility-scale pumped storage hydropower project on
         approximately 400 acres of land. In July 2023, three organizations—Tó Nizhóní Ání, Diné Citizens
         Against Ruining our Environment, and Center for Biological Diversity—submitted a letter to FERC
         attaching resolutions against the project from 18 Navajo Nation chapters and agencies. Nearby
         residents had expressed concerns that the project could damage underground water supplies and
         sacred lands and that the developer had not sufficiently involved nearby residents. In February 2024,
         FERC denied applications for a preliminary permit for the project, stating that “[t]he Commission will
         not issue preliminary permits for projects proposing to use Tribal lands if the Tribes on whose land the
         project is to be located opposes the permit.” 34

     •   Horus Energy AZ 1 LLC’s Prince Road Solar Project (Cochise County): On September 11, 2024, the
         Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission voted to deny a special use permit to construct a 75-
         MW solar farm on 597 acres of land. In voting to deny the project, the commission chairwoman stated,
         “We’ve got too many of these in the county now.”35

     •   SunZia Transmission Line (Cochise County): The SunZia transmission line expects to open in 2026 with
         the ability to carry more than 3,600 MW of wind power generated in New Mexico wind farms. Its
         routing in the San Pedro Valley prompted controversy, with the Tohono O’odham, Hopi, Zuni, and San
         Carlos Apache tribes claiming that the Bureau of Land Management ignored over 15 years of attempts
         by the tribes to recognize the valley as a culturally significant area. In January 2024, the Tohono
         O’odham Nation, San Carlos Apache Tribe, Center for Biological Diversity, and Archeology Southwest
         filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona, claiming that the review of the
         project violated NEPA and the NHPA. The lawsuit was dismissed in June 2024 and subsequently
         appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.36

5. CALIFORNIA




Note on state preemp,on of local restric,ons: On June 30, 2022, the State of California adopted legislaDon
that allows the California Energy Commission to bypass local laws when permiung large-scale renewable
energy projects. Under the new law, the commission has jurisdicDon to issue a cerDﬁcate for any:
(a) photovoltaic solar facility, on-shore wind facility, or thermal energy facility not powered by fossil fuels or
nuclear fuels, with a generaDng capacity of at least 50 MW; (b) energy storage system with a storage capacity
of least 200 MW hours (MWh); (c) electric transmission line from any such generaDng or storage facility to an
interconnected transmission system; and (d) facility that manufactures, produces, or assembles wind, solar, or
storage systems with a capital investment of at least $250,000,000 over a period of 5 years. The law provides
that the issuance of a cerDﬁcate shall “be in lieu of any permit, cerDﬁcate, or similar document required by any




                           Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 24
                                                                                                                         California




state, local, or regional agency,” and “supersede any applicable statute, ordinance, or regulaDon of any state,
local, or regional agency.”40

5.1 State-Level Restric1ons
No restric@ve state laws, regula@ons, or policies were found at this @me.

5.2 Local Restric1ons
     ● City of Escondido (San Diego County): On October 9, 2024, the City of Escondido put in place a 45-day
       moratorium on battery energy storage sites in order to update regulations to account for safety risks.41

     ● Crescent City (Del Norte County): Small wind energy conversion systems are not permitted on vacant
       lots; on a site listed in the National Register of Historic Places or the California Register of Historic
       Resources; where the system would be visible from any coastal scenic resource area; within 100 feet of
       any sensitive or endangered habitat designated by the California Department of Fish and Game
       without written permission from that agency; or within any public right-of-way, easement, path of
       travel, or interior traffic circulation system.42

     ● Los Angeles County: The Los Angeles County Code prohibits “[u]tility-scale wind energy facilities.” The
       code also prohibits ground-mounted utility-scale solar energy facilities in designated areas of ecological
       and economic importance.43

     ● San Bernardino County: In 2019, the San Bernardino County Board of Supervisors banned “utility
       oriented” renewable energy projects in designated “rural living” areas covering more than 1,000,000
       acres of land. Residential solar panels and community solar projects are not affected.44

     ● Santa Clara County: In 2010, Santa Clara County adopted an ordinance that prohibits solar farms from
       land designated as “Agriculture—Large scale”; the ordinance also prohibits solar farms from land

5.3 Contested Projects
       ● Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area First-Generation Wind Farms (Alameda and Contra Costa
         Counties): In 2004, the Center for Biological Diversity brought a lawsuit against the operators of wind
         turbines in the Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, alleging that
         the “obsolete, first-generation wind turbine generators” being used at the site were killing and injuring
         birds in violation of the public trust doctrine. The lawsuit was dismissed, and the dismissal was upheld
         on appeal.46

       ● Aramis Solar Project (Alameda County): Opponents of two North Livermore Valley solar projects,
         Aramis (410 acres) and Sunwalker (70 acres), led by a group called Save North Livermore Valley, argued
         that the proposed locations of the projects impinge on agriculture, natural wildlife habitat, open space,
         and visual and scenic resources. In October 2020, two candidates running for election to the Alameda
         County Board of Supervisors issued a joint statement urging the board to place a moratorium on solar
         development on agricultural land. After the East County Board of Zoning Adjustments approved both
         projects, local groups stated appealed both decisions. By December 2020, three local organizations had
         filed appeals challenging the approval of the Aramis project. In May 2022, the Alameda County
         Superior Court upheld the county’s approval of the Aramis project, dismissing a lawsuit by project
         opponents. In July 2023, Save North Livermore Valley appealed the Superior Court’s decision.
         California’s First District Court of Appeals denied the appeal in August 2023.47

     ● Aratina Solar Center (Kern County): In October 2021, the Kern County Board of Supervisors
       unanimously approved the Aratina Solar Center, a solar-plus-storage project including 530 MW of solar
       capacity and 600 MW of battery energy storage capacity. Shortly thereafter, local community members
       organized a petition that received 51,000 signatures. A primary concern driving local opposition to the
       project is the potential impact on local wildlife and on Joshua Trees. In compliance with the California
       Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act, the developer received an Incidental Take Permit, which
       authorized the developer to remove trees with an option to pay a standard mitigation fee rather than
       complete mitigation fee.48

     ● Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project (Riverside County): The Blythe Mesa Solar Power Project is a 465-
       MW solar farm built between 2010 and 2020 over 4,070 acres of BLM land by the developer NextEra.
       The Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) sued the Department of Interior in 2014 in the U.S. District Court
       for the Central District of California, claiming that BLM’s lack of government-to-government
       consultation violated the NHPA; the lawsuit also included claims under NEPA and the Federal Land
       Policy and Management Act. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the Department
       of Interior in July 2015.49

     ●   Boulder Brush Project (San Diego County): The Boulder Brush Project is a 320-acre substation and
         transmission line proposed by Terra-Gen, which would connect to the 60-turbine Campo Wind Project
         planned for the Campo Indian Reservation. In March 2021, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors
         unanimously approved the project. Residents consequently formed an organization called Backcountry
         Against Dumps to challenge the decision. In April 2021, the organization filed a lawsuit claiming that the
         project violated the California Environmental Quality Act and various planning and zoning regulations. The
         lawsuit contended that the County’s environmental review of the project did not fully analyze the risks to
         wildlife and groundwater and the effects of noise disruptions. In March 2024, the Fourth District Court of Appeal
         vacated the San Diego Superior Court’s dismissal of the lawsuit, instructing the trial court to allow the case to
         proceed.50

     ● BW-IDEOL Offshore Wind Project (Santa Barbara County): In 2022, local conservation groups and
       members of the Northern Chumash Tribe mobilized to oppose the proposed 40-MW BW-IDEOL
       Vandenberg Space Force Base Pilot offshore wind project off the coast of Santa Barbara County, which
       would have consisted of four floating turbines. The project site is in an area the Northern Chumash
       Tribe have sought to designate as a Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary. The company
       withdrew its lease application in February 2023.51

     ● CADEMO Offshore Wind Project (Santa Barbara County): The proposed 60-MW CADEMO
       Demonstration offshore wind project, which is planned to include four floating turbines off the coast of
       Santa Barbara County encountered opposition from local conservation groups and members of the
       Northern Chumash Tribe in 2022. The project site is in an area the Northern Chumash Tribe have
       sought to designate as a Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary. In November 2023, the
       developer entered into a community benefits agreement with the Santa Ynez Chumash to resolve
       opposition to the project.52

     ● Calico Solar Project (San Bernardino County): In 2005, Stirling Energy Systems signed a contract with a
       utility to sell up to 850 MW of energy from a concentrating solar-thermal power plant that would
       involve 30,000 solar dishes standing up to 40 feet high in the Mohave Desert. Due to concerns about
       impacts on the desert tortoise, project plans were reduced to 663.5 MW. In 2012, the Sierra Club,
       Natural Resources Defense Council, and Defenders of Wildlife filed a lawsuit to stop the project,
       arguing that the project was “wrong from the start,” due to impacts on wild lands and wildlife. By
       2013, the project was dead.53

       of the historic Fort Ross. In July 2023, California Senate Majority Leader Mike McGuire stated, “there is
       no chance a project of this size, with this scope, will ever get approval in such an environmentally

     ● Fountain Wind Project (Shasta County): In October 2021, the Shasta County Board of Supervisors
       upheld the Shasta County Planning Commission’s rejection of a permit application for the Fountain
       Wind Project, a 4,500-acre, 200-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen. The project has faced
       significant opposition from the community and from the Pit River Tribe, whose ancestral homelands
       are within the project area. In denying the appeal, supervisors emphasized (a) the height and visibility
       of the turbines and (b) the potential that the presence of turbines could exacerbate the challenge of
       fighting wildfires. In June 2022, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 205 into law, which allowed the
       developer to revive the application and the California Energy Commission to consider overruling the
       decision. In November 2023, Shasta County and the Pit River Tribe filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent
       the Commission from approving the project. The California Attorney General moved for a change of
       venue, citing possible prejudice against the California Energy Commission in the County. In April 2024,
       a Shasta County Superior Court judge denied the request for a change of venue but ruled that a judge
       from another county would preside over the lawsuit.55

     ● Genesis Solar Energy Project (Riverside County): The Genesis Solar Energy Project is a 250-MW

       that the Colorado River Indian Tribe (CRIT) asserted was a historic crematorium, burial ground, and
       village for the Mojave Tribes. After the BLM found no conclusive evidence of habitation, human

     ● Granite Mountain Wind Energy Project (San Bernardino County): The Granite Mountain Wind Energy
       Project was a proposed 84-MW, 100-acre project that Renewable Energy Systems would have built on
       BLM land. The Apple Valley town council and nearby rural communities both expressed opposition to
       the project, based on concerns including impacts to sightlines, property values, and community values.
       A flyer organized by Lucerne Valley residents expressed similar concerns and encouraged individuals to
       submit comments against the project to BLM. In August 2013, the developer withdrew its application
       due to proximity to golden eagle nests.57

     ● Grant Line Solar Project (Alameda County): On September 18, 2022, a local group called Friends of

       Alameda Grant Line Solar 1 project. Friends of Livermore asserted that the project violated Alameda
       County’s “Save Agriculture and Open Lands Initiative,” also known as Measure D. On November 10,
       2022, County Board of Supervisors denied the appeal, allowing the project to move forward.58

     ● Humboldt Wind Energy Area (Humboldt County): In December 2022, the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy

     ● Humidor Battery Energy Storage Project (Los Angeles County): The Humidor Storage Project, a 12-
       acre, 300-MW battery storage facility proposed by Hecate Grid, has faced significant pushback from
       residents of the unincorporated community of Acton in Los Angeles County. Residents have formed
       Save Our Rural Town and Acton Takes Action to campaign against the project and have raised concerns
       about the possibility of leaking chemicals, the threat of facility fires due to the area’s high risk of
       wildfires, and potential impacts on property values. The Acton Town Council has also opposed the
       development of battery storage facilities. In 2022, Los Angeles County approved the site plan for the
       project through an expedited ministerial process. The developer later expanded the project to 400
       MW. Opponents of the project organized a petition and created a website, citing concerns about fire
       risk, environmental impacts, and property values. In September 2023, after an appeal of the county
       approval was denied, Save Our Rural Town filed a lawsuit seeking an injunction to stop the project. In
       April 2024, the same advocacy group submitted comments to the California Energy Commission about
       the project, and the Acton Town Council submitted a request for the California Energy Commission to
       conduct an assessment of public safety concerns. In November 2024, Los Angeles County unanimously
       approved the Humidor storage project.61

     ● Mount Signal Solar Farm (Imperial County): The Mount Signal Solar Farm, also known as the Imperial
       Valley Solar Project, is an 800-MW solar project built by 8minutenergy in Imperial Valley. The project
       was built in three phases beginning in 2011. In November 2010, a three-day protest against the project
       occurred, which included members of Desert Survivors, Basin and Range Watch, Solar Done Right, the
       Quechan Tribe, Cocopah Tribe, Imperial Valley Environmental Justice Task Force, Comite Civico del
       Valle, Seeley Citizens United, and nearby residents. The project was temporarily paused in December
       2010 by a preliminary injunction issued by a judge in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of
       California, in response to a lawsuit filed by the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation. The
       Quechan Tribe’s lawsuit raised claims under NEPA, the NHPA, and the FLPMA.65

     ● Mulqueeney Ranch Wind Repowering Project (Alameda County): In November 2021, the National
       Audubon Society and local affiliates filed a lawsuit in Alameda County Superior Court challenging the
       county’s October 2021 approval of a new 80-MW wind project by Brookfield Renewables in the
       Altamont Pass. The lawsuit alleged insufficient environmental review and failure to adequately assess
       impacts to birds and bats. The lawsuit was eventually resolved by settlement agreement. In March
       2024, the county approved the conditional use permit for the project.66

     ● Napa Sanitation District Solar Farm (Napa County): In May 2024, the Napa Planning Commission voted
       to delay taking action on a proposal to build a 56-acre, 25-MW floating solar farm by Laketricity, at the
       recommendation of county staff. The delay would allow time for the commission to review the public
       comments and deliberate on the proposal. Several groups, including California Unions for Reliable
       Energy, as well as Citizens for Responsible Energy, oppose the project. Opponents have raised concerns
       about wildfire risks and impacts on biological resources. On the other side, a group called Napa Climate

     ● North Sky River Project (Kern County): In October 2012, Defenders of Wildlife, the Center for
       Biological Diversity, and the Sierra Club filed a lawsuit in federal court to block NextEra’s proposal for a
       100-turbine, 300-MW North Sky River Project due to its proximity to California Condor habitat in the
       Tehachapi Mountains. The lawsuit was unsuccessful, and the project was allowed to proceed. As
       completed, the project has a total capacity of 162 MW.68

     ● Panoche Valley Solar Farm (San Benito County): In 2010, San Benito County approved a 399-MW solar
       facility near the town of Hollister. Shortly thereafter, the Sierra Club, the Santa Clara Valley Audubon
       Society, and Save Panoche Valley sued the county, alleging that the project endangered key
       populations of native species. The environmental groups reached a settlement with the developer in
       2019, reducing the size of the project to 130 MW, less than one-third of the original plan.69

     ● Seguro Battery Storage Project (San Diego County): Plans to construct a 320-MW battery energy
       storage system on 22.5 acres of private land in the North County region of San Diego encountered local
       opposition by residents who raised concerns about fire risk and other issues. In November 2023,
       opponents started a change.org petition, which had received approximately 5,000 signatures by the
       end of 2024.70

6.2 Local Restric1ons
     ● Delta County: In September 2022, the Delta County Board of County Commissioners imposed a 6-
       month moratorium on applications for commercial-scale renewable energy facilities. The moratorium
       was later extended, and it was still in effect as of December 2023.78

  Joann K., Commissioners put moratorium on renewable energy projects, DELTA COUNTY CITIZEN REPORT, Sept. 6, 2022,

     ● Mesa County: In January 2024, the Mesa County Board of Commissioners approved a six-month
       moratorium on commercial solar projects in order to provide time to update local zoning regulations.
       The board approved new regulations in April 2024, ending the moratorium.79

     ● Montrose County: In October 2022, the Montrose County Board of County Commissioners imposed a
       6-month moratorium on the processing of applications for power generation facilities. The moratorium
       “does not apply to solar panels or other renewable energy components installed on private residential
       or commercial structures for use within the residential or commercial structure.” In April 2023,
       Montrose County extended the moratorium for 18 months. In December 2024, Montrose County again
       extended the moratorium by another 6 months.80

     ● Rio Blanco County: In August 2023, the Rio Blanco Board of County Commissioners adopted a
       moratorium on wind and solar projects in order to determine how to incorporate such projects into
       the county’s land use plan.81

     ● San Miguel County: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month
       moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was
       scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice. In September 2024, the Board
       unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium. The zoning
       regulations prioritize the siting of solar projects in areas that are already impacted by development.
       Large-scale solar projects of 30 acres or more are only permitted in certain districts and are not
       permitted in the Wright’s Mesa Light Industrial and Wright’s Mesa Rural Agricultural districts.
       Structures on solar farms are also required to be set back at least 200 feet from property lines.82

7. CONNECTICUT




Note on state preemp,on of local restric,ons: The ConnecDcut SiDng Council has exclusive jurisdicDon over
renewable energy faciliDes, excluding certain emergency faciliDes with a capacity of 1 MW or less. While state
law allows local governments to “regulate and restrict the locaDon of a proposed locaDon of a facility,” the
SiDng Council can approve projects that violate local zoning restricDons. The Appellate Court of ConnecDcut
has held that the ConnecDcut SiDng Council “is empowered to review decisions from zoning commissions on a
de novo basis, applying concerns that transcend those involved in local zoning decisions, and that review
may . . . result in the approval of a parDcular site although the facility failed to meet the requirements of local
zoning regulaDons.”90

9. FLORIDA




Note on state preemp,on of local restric,ons: In Florida, a siDng board comprised of the governor and the
governor’s cabinet has the authority to set aside local restricDons on a case-by-case basis. If the siDng board
determines that a proposed facility “does not conform with exisDng land use plans and zoning ordinances,” it
may “authorize a variance or other necessary approval to the adopted land use plan and zoning ordinances
required to render the proposed site or associated facility consistent with local land use plans and zoning
ordinances.” Further, in 2021, Florida enacted legislaDon prevenDng local governments from restricDng solar
energy faciliDes on agricultural land. The law provides that “[a] solar facility shall be a permiWed use in all
agricultural land use categories in a local government comprehensive plan and all agricultural zoning districts
within an unincorporated area.” The law further provides that, although counDes may adopt ordinances
specifying buﬀer and landscaping requirements, any such requirements “may not exceed the requirements for
similar uses involving the construcDon of other faciliDes that are permiWed uses in agricultural land use
categories and zoning districts.”106

10.3 Contested Projects
      ● Cubico Solar Farm in West Bibb County (Bibb County): On May 23, 2022, the Macon-Bibb Planning and
        Zoning Commission unanimously rejected Cubico Sustainable Investments’ plan for a 780-MW solar
        farm, ﬁnding it was not a good ﬁt for the neighborhood where it was proposed. Opponents raised
        concerns about harm to wildlife, damage to roads, and the potenDal for declining property values. In
        the month before the zoning board meeDng, they collected 400 signatures in opposiDon to the
        project.118

      ● SA Solar (Sumter County): In November 2023, the Sumter County Planning & Zoning Board
        recommended that the county Board of Commissioners deny a conditional use permit for SA Solar’s
        proposed solar farm amidst concern about potential aesthetic impacts on a nearby church and
        cemetery. In December 2023, the Board of Commissioners set aside the Planning and Zoning Board’s
        recommendation and granted SA Solar a conditional use permit.119

      ● Silicon Ranch’s Kathleen Solar Project (Houston County): On September 3, 2024, the Houston County
        Commissioners voted to deny a permit to the developer Silicon Ranch to construct a 4,700-acre solar
        farm in Kathleen. The proposal faced opposition from local naturalists due to its proximity to the
        13,450-acre Oaky Woods Wildlife Management Area, which hosts a regionally significant population of
        black bears. The County Attorney stated that the developer would need to wait one year to resubmit
        plans.120

11.2 Local Restric1ons
      ● Honolulu City (Honolulu County): In December 2024, the Honolulu City Council revised the city’s land use
        regulations governing setbacks for wind power. The previous regulations allowed for a 1-to-1 setback
        ratio, while the new regulation increased the required setback distance to 1.25 miles or 10 times the
        height of the wind turbine – whichever is greater – from certain property lines. The Council also
        decided against allowing wind turbines to make repairs affecting their height after the end of their
        contracts.122

11.3 Contested Projects
      ● Kahuku Na Pua Makani Wind Project (Honolulu County): Local opposition to the planned 24-MW Na
        Pua Makani wind project in Kahuku on the North Shore of Oahu reduced the scope of the project from
        13-15 turbines to 8 turbines. In 2016, Keep the North Shore Country filed a contested case hearing
        petition to challenge the developer’s plan for mitigating impacts to endangered species including the
        Hawaiian Hoary Bat. In 2018, the Board of Land and Natural Resources accepted the developer’s plan
        and issued an incidental take license for the project. Keep the North Shore Country appealed that
        decision. In May 2019, the state Circuit Court upheld the state agency’s decision to grant the license,
        and in February 2022, the Supreme Court of Hawaii affirmed on appeal. While this lawsuit was
        pending, Keep the North Shore Country filed a separate petition challenging the proximity of the
        turbines to schools and homes under Honolulu’s zoning ordinance, and an organization called Life of
        the Land filed a motion to block the project’s power purchase agreement. In addition to legal
        challenges, there were significant protests: in October 2019, approximately 128 protesters were
        arrested while trying to block wind turbines from being delivered to the construction site.123

      ● Kawailoa Wind Farm (Honolulu County): In 2018, the 69-MW Kawailoa Wind Farm, operated by
        Kawailoa Wind LLC, sought to amend its Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) and Incidental Take License
        (ITL) to account for higher-than-anticipated incidental take of the endangered Hawaiian hoary bat. In
        2019, the state Board of Land and Natural Resources (BLNR) approved the proposed amendments. The
        environmental group Keep the North Shore Country (KNSC), challenged the amendments as being
        inadequate to address the wind farm’s impacts on wildlife. The BLNR granted KNSC a contested case
        hearing to formally present their objections. In January 2021, the parties reached a settlement and
        entered into an agreement in which Kawaiola agreed to fund an enhanced research plan to provide
        greater protections to endangered species.124

      ● Bannock County: In October 2023, the Bannock County Board of Commissioners enacted a 180-day
        moratorium on permits for large-scale energy projects. Then, in March 2024, the board enacted an
        ordinance that bans solar farms capable of producing 10 MW or more of energy, storing 10 MW or
        more of energy, or which encompass 100 or more acres of land. The ordinance also categorically bans
        commercial-scale wind turbines and limits non-commercial wind turbines to two turbines per lot.126

13. ILLINOIS




Note on state preemp,on of local restric,ons: On January 27, 2023, Illinois enacted Public Law 102-1123,
which sets limits on counDes’ authority to restrict or otherwise regulate renewable energy faciliDes. First, the
law prohibits counDes from establishing moratoriums on wind or solar projects. Second, the law establishes
statewide siDng parameters and prohibits counDes from adopDng limits more restricDve than those
parameters. For example, under the new state law, counDes are no longer permiWed to impose: (1) setbacks
from property lines in excess of 1.1 Dmes the blade Dp height of a commercial wind turbine or 50 feet from a
commercial solar project; (2) setbacks from nonparDcipaDng residences in excess of 2.1 Dmes the blade Dp
height of a commercial wind turbine or 150 feet from a commercial solar project; or (3) restricDons on shadow




                          Sabin Center for Climate Change Law | Opposition to Renewable Energy in the United States | 71
                                                                                                                          Illinois




ﬂicker to less than 30 hours per year. This law likely renders all of the local restricDons described below
invalid.135

13.1 State-Level Restric1ons
      •   Senate Bill 1127: In June 2023, Senate Bill 1127 was signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker after passing
          through the House and Senate without opposition. SB 1127 prevents future solar and wind
          development in the Lee-Ogle Enterprise Zone, a 2,000-acre area in and southeast of Rochelle.136

13.2 Local Restric1ons
      ● Christian County: In September 2020, the Christian County Board voted 10-6 to approve zoning code
        amendments with restrictive setback and shadow flicker requirements. The regulations were
        interpreted as effectively banning wind farms in the county. Following the adoption of Public Act 102-
        1123 (2023), the ordinance was revised to provide that, if any of these restrictions were judicially
        determined to violate state law, then the limits set out in PA 102-1123 would apply.137

      ● DeKalb County: In 2018, DeKalb County passed an ordinance that requires wind turbines to be set back
        from property lines by a distance of 6 Dmes turbine height and 3 miles from any municipality. The
        ordinance also requires that zero shadow ﬂicker occur beyond property lines and that wind projects not
        increase background noise levels by more than 5 dBA. These restricDons were removed to achieve
        compliance with Public Act 102-1123 (2023).138

      ● Ford County: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its
        ordinance. In 2018, the county board’s zoning commiWee recommended increasing the exisDng 1,000-
        foot setback from buildings to 2,250 feet. At a hearing in October 2018, a group called Ford County
        CiDzens for Property Rights demanded 3,250-foot setbacks from any property lines. On September 13,
        2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet
        from property lines upon which a primary structure is located. The ordinance further speciﬁed that,

      ● Village of Teutopolis (Effingham County): In June 2023, the Village of Teutopolis banned the
        construction of wind farms within the village’s corporate limits and extraterritorial jurisdictional
        limits.144

13.3 Contested Projects
      ● Alexis Solar Project (Mercer County): Mercer County residents have expressed opposition to a 380-
        acre solar farm that Birch Creek Energy has proposed for Alexis, Illinois. At an October 2023 meeting
        with the Mercer County Zoning Board, some residents expressed concerns about loss of farmland.
        Local opposition also focused on concerns about noise and environmental impacts, including impacts
        to endangered species. The Mercer County Zoning Board denied Birch Creek’s conditional use permit
        application in November 2023.145

      ● Alta Wind Farm (DeWitt County): The Alta Wind Farm was approved in July 2020 by the DeWitt
        County Board despite local opposition. The 200-MW project had been proposed nearly 10 years
        before. In October 2020, opponents filed two separate lawsuits to stop the project but dropped both
        of those lawsuits in March 2021. In July 2021, the DeWitt County Board approved a motion preventing
        the issuance of new building permits to Enel Green Power for the Alta Wind Farm until the company
        could prove that its turbines could be curtailed during severe weather events. An Illinois judge then
        issued a mandamus order holding that the Dewitt County Board lacked legal authority to halt the
        issuance of building permits. The wind farm proceeded to operation in June 2023.146

      ● Amp Solar’s Pratt Road Solar Garden (DeKalb County): On May 1, 2023, the Sandwich City Council
        issued a resolution asking the DeKalb County Board to reject plans for a 5-MW, 76-acre solar farm on
        the periphery of the city. The resolution stated that the project, if approved, would unduly constrain
        the city’s growth.147

      ● Bundleflower Solar LLC (Livingston County): In February 2023, the City of Pontiac Planning and Zoning
        Board denied the application of Bundleflower Solar LLP for a rezoning, special-use permit, and variance
        in order to install a solar farm. The applicant had requested to decrease the 1,500-foot setback
        requirement to a 100-foot setback to enable the construction of a 5,568-panel project. Soon after the
        Board’s decision, Bundleflower withdrew its application for the solar farm.148

      ● Ford Ridge Wind Farm (Ford County): In March 2021, the Ford Ridge Wind Farm received the

      ● Goose Creek Wind Project / Prosperity Wind Farm (Piatt County): On February 3, 2023, the Piatt
        County Zoning Board of Appeals voted against recommending a zoning permit for Apex Clean Energy’s
        300-MW, 50-turbine Goose Creek wind project. This followed 14 nights of hearings in November and
        December. Opponents of the project emphasized health issues, shadow flicker, the loss of farmland,
        and the lack of need for additional energy in the community. In October 2023, citing intervening
        changes in Illinois law, the Piatt County Board approved the project, which, by then, had been renamed
        Prosperity Wind Farm.150

      ● Grain Belt Express (Christian, Clark, Cumberland, Greene, Macoupin, Montgomery, Pike, Scott, and
        Shelby Counties): In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of clean energy
        high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border. The
        Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) first approved it in 2015. Landowner and agriculture groups called
        Concerned Citizens and Property Owners, Illinois Agricultural Association, and Landowners Alliance of
        Central Illinois challenged the approval in state court, and, in 2018, an Illinois appellate court
        overturned the approval on the grounds that regulators improperly allowed the company to use an
        expedited review process. The project was eventually bought in 2020 by Invenergy, but the previous
        court order still prevented the project from going forward. In 2022, Gov. J.B. Pritzker signed the
        Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which enabled construction to proceed despite the court’s ruling. The
        ICC approved the project for the second time in March 2023, allowing Invenergy to start building the
        HVDC power line. In August 2023, an Illinois appellate court enacted a stay on implementation of the
        March 2023 order to decide its constitutionality, but the court lifted the stay in September 2023. In
        August 2023, an Illinois appellate court enacted a stay on implementation of the March 2023 order to
        decide the project’s constitutionality. In September 2023, the court lifted the stay allowing the
        developer to continue with planning while the appeal moves forward. In August 2024, the Illinois
        appellate court reversed the ICC’s March 2023 approval of the project, citing issues with the financing
        of the project. In November 2024, the state’s Supreme Court granted leave to hear the appeal of the
        appellate court’s ruling.151

      ● Harvest Ridge Wind Farm (Douglas County): In June 2018, residents of Newman Township voted 86-57
        in favor of enacting a zoning ordinance to block the proposed 200-MW Harvest Ridge Wind Farm. The
        Douglas County Board, however, approved the project. In July 2020, the project was completed.152

      ● Radford’s Run Wind Farm (Macon County): In 2015, three dozen landowners filed a lawsuit to halt the
        139-turbine, 305-MW Radford’s Run Wind Farm, arguing that the “county did not properly provide
        statutory notices for a public hearing leading up to the board’s decision or allow them to view the wind
        farm applications in time for the hearing.” The suit was dismissed, and the project was ultimately
        constructed in 2017.158

      ● SolarStone Partners Solar Farm (Tazewell County): In February 2023, the Tazewell County Board
        unanimously rejected a zoning change that would have allowed SolarStone Partners to establish a solar
        farm near Illinois Central Christian School. The board also voted against a zoning change that would
        have brought a wind farm to the county.159

      ● Top Hat Wind Project (Logan County): As of November 2022, over 1,000 people had signed a petition
        opposing plans for the 200-MW, 60-turbine Top Hat Wind Project over concerns about interference
        with radar. That same month, however, after the developers entered into an agreement with the
        National Weather Service to shut off the turbines in case of severe weather, the Logan County Board
        approved the project. Opponents, including a group called Logan County Residents Against the Top Hat
        Wind Factory, stated that they were considering filing a lawsuit.160

      ● Will County Solar Farm (Will County): On September 10, 2024, the Will County Land Use and
        Development Committee voted unanimously to deny a special use permit to construct a 300-MW solar
        project on 3,600 acres of land in Custer and Reed townships. The developer ACCIONA Energia

      ● Allen County: According to the Allen County zoning ordinance, last updated in September 2019, wind
        energy conversion systems with any of the following three characterisDcs are prohibited: (a) a
        nameplate capacity of more than 50 kW; (b) a total height of more than 60 feet; and (c) a total swept
        area of more than 40 feet.162

      ● Boone County: Boone County banned wind farms in or around 2009 ager wind energy developers
        approached the county about potenDal development opportuniDes. In April 2024, the Boone County
        Board of Commissioners adopted a new 2-year moratorium on large-scale solar, wind, and storage

      ● Clark County: In November 2024, the Clark County Commission issued new requirements for solar
        projects. The County has imposed a cap of 4,000 acres of “fenced area” that can be devoted to solar in
        the county. The county increased setback requirements for solar arrays, inverters, and power
        substations from the nearest non-participation residential dwellings to 650 feet for solar arrays, 650
        feet for inverters, and 1,250 feet for power substations.164

      ● Clinton County: Clinton County upheld a moratorium on wind farms in September 2019.165

      ● Delaware County: On February 22, 2022, the Delaware County Commissioners approved amendments

        200 feet and classifying solar as a “special use” subject to public hearings and addiDonal approvals. The
        County Commissioners also enacted a 1-year moratorium on solar farm development; in August 2023,
        the Commissioners extended this moratorium through the end of 2023. The amendments and
        moratorium followed intense local opposiDon to the proposed Meadow Forge solar project.166

        farms are prohibited in all unincorporated areas of Fulton County. Previously, wind farms were banned

      ● Hamilton County: Under the Uniﬁed Development Ordinance of 2022, wind turbines must not exceed
        300 feet in height and must be set back by at least 1.5 Dmes the tower height from property lines;
        commercial solar projects are prohibited on prime agricultural soils and must be set back at least 300
        feet from neighboring houses. For some period in 2019, there was a moratorium on wind projects.168

      ● Henry County: As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed
        resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built. These buffers extend
        approximately 4 miles around each town. The twelve towns included Cadiz, Sulphur Springs, Kennard,
        Blountsville, Greensboro, Lewisville, Mount Summit, Springport, Straughn, and Middletown. In May
        2019, Indiana passed a law limiting municipalities’ authority to enact such buffer zones going forward
        and voiding any such ordinances or resolution adopted after December 31, 2018. The law did not void
        any ordinances or resolutions adopted before January 1, 2019. Eleven of the Henry County town
        resolutions were grandfathered in under the law, but the town of Middletown’s was not.169

      ● Howard County: In 2015, Howard County adopted amendments to a wind ordinance that increased
        setback requirements from 1,500 feet to 2,000 feet from the nearest property and decreased the noise
        limit from 50 dBA to 40 dBA.170

      ● Kosciusko County: In January 2019, Kosciusko County adopted a 60-day moratorium on permits for
        large-scale solar projects, which was extended by 90 days in March 2019. Kosciusko’s zoning
        ordinance, last updated in January 2022, only allows commercial solar as an exceptional use in heavy
        industrial districts and disallows commercial solar in all other districts. Kosciusko County’s zoning
        ordinance also requires wind turbine setbacks of at least 3,960 feet or 6.5 times the turbine height
        from property lines, limits turbine noise to 32 dBA, requires zero shadow flicker effects on neighboring
        homes, and limits construction to dedicated industrial zones.172

      ● Lake County: Lake County’s solar ordinance, passed in April 2016, disallows ground-mounted solar as a
        primary land use throughout the county. Ground-mounted solar is permitted only as an accessory use
        throughout the county.173

      ● Madison County: In December 2023, the Madison County Board of Commissioners unanimously
        approved a solar ordinance that requires solar farms to be set back 3 miles from waterways and other
        solar farms and that limits solar farms to 400 acres in size. Madison County previously imposed a
        moratorium on solar development from 2021 unDl the adopDon of the December 2023 ordinance. In
        March 2024, the Madison County Board of Commissioners passed a resoluDon imposing an indeﬁnite
        moratorium on all new wind faciliDes, with the stated intenDon of reviewing the county’s wind
        ordinance within a year.174

      ● Marshall County: In or around 2013, Marshall County commissioners voted unanimously to ban all
        commercial wind development. The prohibiDon remains in eﬀect as of the latest version of the zoning
        ordinance available online in February 2023.175

      ● Miami County: In 2018, Miami County increased wind turbine setbacks to 2,000 feet from property
        lines and roadways amidst local opposiDon to a proposed 75-turbine project in the northern part of the
        county. Under the 2021 version of the ordinance, wind turbines must be set back 0.5 miles from rivers
        or reservoirs.176

      ● Montgomery County: A 2019 Zoning Ordinance renders it eﬀecDvely impossible to construct wind
        farms in Montgomery County. The ordinance calls for setbacks from property lines or roads of either 5
        Dmes the turbine height or 2,640 feet (which may be increased to 3,200 feet at the zoning board’s
        discreDon). It also requires setbacks of 1 mile from a town or school, a maximum of 32 dBA, and zero
        shadow ﬂicker. Property values must be guaranteed for residents within 2 miles of any turbine, and
        commercial turbine construcDon is limited to industrial districts.177

      ● Noble County: Since 2013, Noble County has required a 3,960-foot setback from property lines for
        wind projects.178

      ● Posey County: In January 2021, the Posey County Commission voted to prohibit all turbines within 10

        Posey County mandates that no ground-mounted solar system may be closer than 1 mile to any
        municipal boundary line. The Ordinance also mandates that no wind energy project may be located

        property line of a non-participating property.183

        wind energy systems with a capacity greater than 50 kW or a total height of more than 100 feet are
        “not a permiWed use.” While the ordinance sets out a procedure for small wind energy systems to
        obtain permission as special excepDons, the ordinance does not appear to provide a similar procedure
        for large systems.188

      ● Aypa Solar Project (Jefferson County): In September 2024, the Madison City Council voted to deny a
        rezoning proposal that would have allowed the proposed Aypa Power solar farm to proceed in
        Madison, Indiana. Residents expressed concerns about buffer zones and impacts on the environment
        and wildlife.191

      ● Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm (Henry County): The Henry County Planning Commission rejected a
        proposal for the Big Blue Ribbon Wind Farm in 2019 amidst community opposition to the project.
        Residents raised concerns about health impacts and property rights, arguing that a 1,500-foot setback
        from homes was not sufficient.192

      ● BrightNight Solar Project (Clark County): In October 2023, the Clark County Board of Zoning Appeals
        denied a special exemption permit for a 3,900-acre solar project proposed by developer BrightNight.
        The permit was necessary because the project would have been built on agricultural land. Residents
        opposed the project on the basis of potential impacts to viewsheds.193

      ● Carina Solar (Bartholomew County): Plans to construct the 100-MW Carina Solar project on 1,880
        acres of land under Bartholomew County and City of Columbus jurisdiction encountered opposition
        from a local group Nonprofit Bartholomew County Citizens Concerned about Commercial Solar Fields
        (B4CSF). In February 2024, the Bartholomew County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a conditional use
        permit for the 1,100-acre piece the project that would be sited within its jurisdiction. That same
        month, the City of Columbus Board of Zoning Appeals approved an application for a separate 800 acres
        piece. The developer filed a lawsuit appealing the county’s denial, while local opponents filed a lawsuit
        appealing the city’s approval. The Bartholomew Circuit Court consolidated the two lawsuits in June. On
        July 30, 2024, the developer withdrew its application as part of a stipulation dismissing the litigation.194

      ● Cold Spring Solar Farm (Putnam County): In September 2023, following fourteen months of
        negotiations, the Putnam County Board of Zoning Appeals denied a motion for a special exception to
        permit the 200-MW Cold Spring Solar Farm in Russell Township. The decision was largely based on the
        project’s planned utilization of 1,400 acres of farmland, and the decision received support from
        residents seeking to preserve the Township’s rural character.195

      ● Elkhart County Solar Project (Elkhart County): In October 2021, Elkhart County commissioners voted
        against rezoning agricultural land for a 150-MW solar energy project near Millersburg, Indiana. The
        project had previously earned the support of the Elkhart County Council, the county Plan Commission,
        and the Economic Development Corp. However, the commissioners sided with neighbors who opposed
        the project because of potential decreases in property values and visual impacts. However, in
        September 19, 2022, Elkhart County approved a zoning change for a revised 100-MW version of the
        project. 196

      ● Flat Rock Wind Project (Rush County): In May 2015, the Rush County Board of Zoning Appeals

15. IOWA




Note on state preemp,on of local restric,ons: In Iowa, a cerDﬁcate from the state uDliDes board is required
for electric generaDng faciliDes with a capacity of 25 MW or more. The law provides that “[t]he failure of a
facility to meet zoning requirements” established by ciDes or counDes “shall not preclude the board from
issuing the cerDﬁcate.” However, as a pracDcal maWer, experts of the Iowa siDng process have stated that local
zoning cannot be preempted.215

15.2 Local Restric1ons
      ● Adams County: In September 2024, Adams County adopted wind regulations that cap total wind
        turbines in the county to 225 turbines and require turbines to be set back at least 1.5 times turbine
        height from property lines.216

      ● Adair County: In November 2019, the County’s Board of Supervisors capped the number of commercial
        wind turbines allowed in the county at 535 turbines. At the time, there were already 532 turbines
        either built or under construction.217

      ● Butler County: Last amended in November 2022, Butler County’s zoning ordinance for unincorporated
        areas includes a number of restrictions on wind development. Commercial wind turbines must be set
        back 1,640 feet from participating property lines and 1,800 feet from non-participating property lines.
        Commercial wind turbines must also remain below 40 dBa.218

      ● Cerro Gordo County: In May 2023, the Cerro Gordo County Board of Supervisors passed a 15-month
        moratorium on utility-scale solar and wind energy, along with battery storage facilities, in order to
        consider regulations for future permitting of such facilities. In December 2024, the Cerro Gordo Board
        of Supervisors voted unanimously to pass a moratorium on the installation of new utility-scale solar,
        wind and battery-energy storage systems located on land zoned for agricultural use.219

      ● City of Council Bluffs (Pottawattamie County): Since 2009, wind energy conversion systems, such as
        wind turbines and windmills, have been prohibited within the City of Council Bluffs.220

      ● Clinton County: On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a
        three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008

      ● Montgomery County: In July 2022, Montgomery County passed a 1-year moratorium on wind energy
        development. Montgomery County approved a 180-day extension on the moratorium in June 2023. In
        November 2023, the county extended the moratorium indefinitely.234

      ● Muscatine County: In January 2024, the Muscatine County Board of Supervisors passed a 9-month
        moratorium on the issuance of special use permits for commercial wind farms, in order to provide time
        for the Board to consult wind farm experts and potentially promulgate revised ordinances.235

      ● Page County: In March 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors imposed a moratorium on
        commercial wind applications while it considers changes to its ordinance.236

      ● Palo Alto County: On June 22, 2022, the Palo Alto County Board of Supervisors adopted revisions to
        the county wind ordinance that set a countywide limit for wind energy production of 600 MW and
        required that turbines be set back from Rush Lake and Virgin Lake by 0.5 miles.237

      ● Pottawattamie County: In February 2024, the Pottawattamie County Board of Supervisors adopted
        new wind and solar zoning restrictions. Under the new zoning ordinance, wind turbines must not
        exceed 412 feet in height; new solar farms must be set back at least a quarter mile (402 meters) from
        property lines; and new solar farms must be set back at least a half mile (804 meters) from
        residences.238

      ● Ringgold County: In July 2023, the Ringgold County Board of Supervisors approved new ordinances for
        wind turbines and solar. The wind ordinance requires that commercial wind turbines must be set back
        at least 0.5 miles (2,640 feet) from adjoining property lines, roads, and certain parks and public areas

      ● Sac County: Sac County’s wind energy regulations limit shadow flicker on any human-occupied
        dwelling to 20 hours per year. The regulations require that wind towers be set back the greater of 3.5
        times turbine height or 1,697 feet from the nearest residential dwelling, incorporated areas, public
        recreational areas, village residential areas, lake area development districts, urban transition districts,
        and event centers. The setback from a dwelling can be reduced to the height of the tower if the
        property owner signs a written waiver. The regulation also establishes a setback of 1.5 times turbine
        height from non-participating property lines, unless the property owner signs a written waiver.240

      ● Sioux County: In September 2022, Sioux County adopted a 1-year moratorium on commercial wind
        development. Sioux County extended the wind energy moratorium for another year in September
        2023 and also enacted a moratorium on commercial solar projects.241

      ● Union County: In March 2023, the Union County Board of Supervisors extended an industrial wind
        energy moratorium until December 2023. A group called “Protect Our Land’s Future” had argued that
        the current county setback of 1,500 feet between a turbine and a structure did not adequately protect
        other uses of property. The moratorium was again extended until its eventual expiration in July 2024,
        when the county adopted changes to its wind ordinance. The county’s new wind ordinance requires
        that wind turbines be set back the greater of 0.62 miles (3,281 feet) or 7 times turbine height from a
        property line.242

      ●   Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm (Freemont and Page Counties): In August 2022, the Page County Board
          of Supervisors initially approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of
          opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning
          agreements. Just over a month after the approval, residents opposed to the project filed a lawsuit
          against the county and board in state court, which was later removed to federal court. In February
          2023, after the developer informed the Board of Supervisors that it would be removing 3 turbines from
          the plan, the Page County Zoning Administrator informed the developer that this was a “material
          change,” which rendered the application “void” and revoked the permit. The developer appealed the
          Zoning Administrator’s decision to the Page County Board of Adjustment. In March 2023, the Board of
          Adjustment upheld the revocation of the permit. A week later, the developer filed a lawsuit against the
          County officials in federal court challenging the revocation. In May 2024, the federal court denied the
          residents’ state claims which had been rendered moot at the time the permit was revoked. In
          November 2024, in a 2-1 vote, the Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to enter into a
          settlement agreement resolving the pending litigation and allowing the developer to proceed with
          construction of the project.253

16. KANSAS




16.1 State-Level Restric1ons
      ● Tallgrass Heartland Wind Moratorium: In 2004, Kansas Governor Kathleen Sebelius instated a wind
        development moratorium on parts of the Flint Hills in order to protect the tallgrass prairie. In 2011,
        Governor Sam Brownback doubled the protected area, renaming it the “Tallgrass Heartland.” This
        moratorium, which covers parts of 12 counties, was continued in July 2020 by Governor Laura Kelly.257

16.2 Local Restric1ons
      •   Barton County: In May 2023, the Barton County Commission voted to require any solar farm to be 6
          miles away from Cheyenne Bottoms—a wetland complex with significant wildlife—and placed a
          moratorium on commercial solar projects until the end of the year. In March 2024, the Commission
          approved an amendment to the zoning regulations, updating the zoning map of Barton County to

      ● Anderson County Wind Farm (Anderson County): In 2015, Calpine CorporaDon proposed a 200-MW
        wind project on 30,000 acres on a ridge in Eastern Anderson County. A group called Landowners
        Against Windmills organized in opposiDon. The group argued that the county’s zoning director
        unlawfully allowed Calpine to construct a 328-foot weather monitoring tower without a special use
        permit, violaDng public noDce requirements. The tower was subsequently destroyed by vandalism at a
        loss of $200,000. The project was apparently abandoned. As of February 2023, there are no Calpine
        projects in Kansas or public plans to build in Anderson County.279

      ● Argyle Creek Wind Project (Sumner County): In January 2017, nearly 60 residents of Sumner County
        ﬁled a lawsuit to challenge the county’s approval of a condiDonal use permit for the 60-turbine, 150-
        MW Argyle Creek Wind Farm. In September 2017, a judge ruled against the Sumner County
        Commission, thereby blocking the project.280

      ● Auburn Harvest Wind (Osage County): In October 2022, Osage County Commissioners denied an
        applicaDon from Auburn Harvest Wind to construct a wind farm on 30,000 acres. At a hearing earlier in
        the month, local residents expressed concerns that the project would permanently alter the landscape
        and impact wildlife.281

        energy projects exceeding 40 acres.282

17.1 State-Level Restric1ons
       •   House Bill 291 of 2014: Under House Bill 291, adopted in 2014, wind turbines must be set back at least
           1,000 feet from property lines and at least 2,000 feet from “any residential neighborhood, school,
           hospital, or nursing home facility.”289

       •   Boyle County: Boyle County prohibits ground-mounted solar panel systems from being the primary use
           of a property in an agricultural district if the property is smaller than ten acres.290

      •   City of Hopkinsville (Christian County): Hopkinsville’s solar ordinance requires that certain large-scale
          solar projects be set back at least 1,000 feet from any lot line and at least 2,000 feet from the nearest
          lot line of any property containing a residential use or quasi-public use.291

      •   Lyon County: In May 2024, Lyon County passed a solar ordinance that establishes a 2,000-foot setback
          for large-scale solar projects from any non-participating property line and any right-of-way for a
          publicly maintained roadway or rail-line.292

      •   Mason County: Mason County’s solar ordinance mandates that utility-scale solar projects be set back
          at least 500 feet from private property lines, and at least 600 or 750 feet from dwellings, schools, and
          many other occupied buildings, depending on the size of the property.293

      •   Meade County: Meade County’s solar ordinance mandates that no more than 2,000 acres in the
          unincorporated areas of the county may be used for “Level 3” (large scale) solar.294

      •   Villa Hills (Kenton County): Villa Hills has banned commercial solar projects by requiring in its solar
          ordinance that the primary purpose of solar energy systems be for providing power for the property
          where the system is located, rather than for commercial use. It also requires that solar panels on flat
          roofs in non-residential zones not be visible from public rights-of-way, parking lots, and adjacent
          properties.295

19.1 State-Level Restric1ons
      •   Bill L.D. 1619: In July 2021, Governor Janet Mills signed into law L.D. 1619, sponsored by Senator Mark
          Lawrence. With some exceptions, the law permanently banned the development of all offshore wind
          projects in Maine state waters but allowed the permitting of offshore wind in federal waters if the
          Governor’s Energy Office developed a planned research strategy for such projects by March 2023. The
          law also created the Offshore Wind Research Consortium (ORWC) to study the effects of offshore wind
          energy on the Gulf of Maine. The law was supported by Maine lobstermen, who expressed concerns
          about the impact of offshore wind on the state’s fishing industry.309

          which is planned to transmit power from a new large wind project in Northern Maine. Residents
          expressed concerns that the project would disrupt farmland and disorient bees through electric and
          magnetic fields.314

          wind ordinance requiring a 1-mile setback from all non-parDcipaDng properDes.322

      •   Town of Freedom (Waldo County): In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine
          ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource.
          Depending on the height and megawaW capacity of the turbine, the ordinance requires it be setback
          either 1.5 Dmes turbine height, 3 Dmes turbine height, or 13 Dmes turbine height from non-
          parDcipaDng landowners. Turbines less than 100 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in
          capacity must be set back at least 1.5 Dmes turbine height; turbines between 100 and 150 feet in
          height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 3 Dmes turbine height; and
          turbines greater than 150 feet in height and/or greater than 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least
          13 Dmes turbine height. The ordinance measures turbine height by the highest point of any turbine
          blade Dp. Shadow ﬂicker is limited to ten hours per year, and depending on the Dme of day and height
          of turbine, noise is limited to between 30 and 40 dBa.323

      •   Town of Glenburn (Penobscot County): In April 2021, the Town of Glenburn imposed a 2-month
          moratorium on commercial solar faciliDes. Then, in March 2022, Glenburn banned solar faciliDes larger
          than 15,000 square feet.324

19.3 Contested Projects
      ● Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project (Kennebec and Waldo Coun>es): The Aroostook Renewable
        Gateway Project is a 150-mile, 1,200-MW transmission corridor designed to transmit energy from the
        proposed 170-turbine King Pine Wind Farm in Aroostook County to consumers in southern Maine and
        MassachuseWs. LS Power was iniDally developing the project. In June 2023, Maine adopted a bill
        approving the project, but the project has been slowed by local opposiDon and moratoria. Maine
        residents opposing the project have raised concerns about impacts to property and sightlines, formed a
        ciDzen group called Preserve Rural Maine, and obtained legal counsel. In August 2023, in response to
        this project, the town of Albion imposed a 6-month moratorium on uDlity lines and corridors, with
        residents expressing concerns that the project would disrupt farmland and that the project’s
        electromagneDc ﬁelds would disorient bees. Also, in response to the project, in September 2023, the
        Town of Palermo adopted a transmission line moratorium. In November 2023, the Town of Unity
        adopted a 180-day moratorium on high-voltage power lines. In December 2023, LS Power announced
        that it could no longer proceed with the project at the agreed-upon price. In response, the Maine
        Public UDliDes Commission announced that it was terminaDng its agreement with LS Power and
        delaying development unDl it could ﬁnd another developer for the project. However, in October 2024,
        the Department of Energy announced a $425 million capacity contract with Avangrid to restart
        conversaDons with the Maine PUC on conDnuing the transmission project. In November 2024, the
        Town of China’s select board passed a 180-day High-Impact Electric Transmission Line Moratorium
        Ordinance in response to the project.340

      ● Bingham Wind (Piscataquis County): An anD-wind group called Friends of Maine’s Mountains ﬁled a
        lawsuit against developer SunEdison to stop construcDon of the 185-MW Bingham Wind project. In
        2015, the parDes reached a seWlement in which SunEdison agreed not to develop projects in exclusion
        zones covering more than half of the state and to pay up to $2.5 million for conservaDon projects
        statewide.341

      ● Bower’s Mountain Wind Farm (Penobscot County): In December 2015, the Maine Supreme Judicial
        Court aﬃrmed the ruling of the Maine Board of Environmental ProtecDon that rejected SunEdison’s
        permit for the $100 million Bowers Mountain Wind Farm. The project would have consisted of 16
        turbines generaDng a total of 48 MW. Local advocacy groups opposed the project due to potenDal
        interference with views of nearby lakes. In aﬃrming the Board’s ruling, the Maine Supreme Judicial
        Court cited the statutory requirement that a wind project not unreasonably compromise views in
        certain scenic areas.342

      ● Bull Hill Wind Project (Hancock County): In 2011, the local organization Concerned Citizens of Rural
        Hancock County (CCRHC) intervened in a public evidentiary hearing before the Land Use Regulation
        Commission (LURC) to challenge developer Blue Sky East, LLC’s request for a permit to build the 19-
        turbine, 34-MW Bull Hill Wind Project. The opponents argued that the wind farm would ruin the
        landscape and threaten wildlife while generating very little electricity. The LURC approved the project
        after imposing more stringent noise requirements and requiring a community benefits package of
        $4,000 per turbine per year.343
